corrections.compiler_and_flags: hipcc ($ROCM_PATH/bin/hipcc) inside the ROCm 7.0 preview image the README names (rocm/7.0-preview:rocm7.0_preview_pytorch_training_mi35x_beta); analysis/attn/bkwd/benchmark/Makefile builds the kernels as pybind11 extensions with -DKITTENS_CDNA4 --offload-arch=gfx950 -DHIP_ENABLE_WARP_SYNC_BUILTINS -ffast-math -std=c++20 -w -shared -fPIC (no explicit -O level in that Makefile; the newer kernels/common.mk adds -O3). test_python.py: 500 warmup and 100 timed iterations with torch.cuda events, BF16. corrections.claimed_speedup: GQA non-causal backward (B=16, 64 Q heads, 8 KV heads, D=128) on MI355X, from benchmark/mi355x_gqa_bkwd_non_causal.json and plot.py: HipKittens 881 / 1007 / 1106 / 1155 / 1176 TFLOPS at N = 1024 / 2048 / 4096 / 8192 / 16384 vs AITER 300 / 351 / 375 / 384 / 389, Composable Kernel 368 / 428 / 447 / 463 / 465 and PyTorch SDPA 220 / 273 / 301 / 309 / 312; 2.93x to 3.02x over AITER (derived from page data). GQA causal backward: 2.98x to 4.33x over AITER (588 vs 151 TFLOPS at N=1024, 995 vs 334 at 16384; derived from page data). The win is GQA-specific: for MHA (B=16, H=16, D=128) HipKittens is at parity or slower than AITER beyond short sequences: non-causal 734 vs 590 (1.24x) at N=1024, 1027 vs 1056 (0.97x) at 4096, 1119 vs 1201 (0.93x) at 16384; causal 462 vs 389 (1.19x) at 1024, 941 vs 1034 (0.91x) at 8192, 1028 vs 1109 (0.93x) at 16384 (derived from benchmark/mi355x_mha_bkwd_*.json).
corrections.caveats: Baselines are AMD libraries (AITER, hipBLASLt, Composable Kernel) plus Triton and PyTorch, none of which are in the category's baseline list (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor), and this is a GPU kernel library, so it fits the category only loosely. The roughly 3x attention-backward win holds only for GQA; on MHA backward the same harness shows HipKittens 3-9% slower than AITER from N=2048-4096 upward (benchmark/mi355x_mha_bkwd_non_causal.json and mi355x_mha_bkwd_causal.json), which suggests AITER's GQA backward path, not its tuned MHA path, is what HipKittens beats by 3x. Timing is not symmetric: AITER is timed as one autograd out.backward(dO) call through PyTorch (dispatch overhead and any GQA dK/dV reduction included), while HipKittens times its three kernels (prep, combined backward, dQ shuffle) directly. In plot.py the PyTorch SDPA values for the GQA plots are identical to the MHA values (220.27 / 273.06 / ... non-causal, 109.51 / 156.71 / ... causal), so the PyTorch bars in the GQA figures were copied, not measured on GQA shapes. The GQA N=16384 lines in mi355x_benchmark.sh are commented out (with ATTN_B=15), so how that JSON row was produced is not shown. HipKittens gradients differ from AITER within BF16 rounding (max abs error 0.0039; 103 dK and 1452 dV elements outside a 0.001 + 5% tolerance at N=1024). The BF16 GEMM plot (analysis/bf16_gemm) shows parity with AMD's libraries rather than a win (numbers from the search record, not re-checked here). Baseline numbers were collected by the authors in October/November 2025 and the README warns the frameworks keep evolving; AITER now includes HipKittens kernels (March 2026), so a re-run may differ. The paper (arXiv 2511.08083, MLSys 2026) and the Hazy Research and AMD blogs could not be opened (hosts blocked).

notes: Numbers re-derived exactly from the committed JSON (HK and AITER) and plot.py (CK times converted with the script's FLOP formula, PyTorch hard-coded). Headline is the best case: HipKittens loses slightly to AITER on MHA backward at N>=4096, and the PyTorch bars in the GQA plots reuse MHA values. Record shortcoming: GQA-only win, asymmetric timing, copied PyTorch baseline values.

tier_reason: The only evidence is the peer-reviewed ACM TOMS 45(4) 2019 paper cited in the README; search results confirm it benchmarks CoDiPack's four tape types against Adept and ADOL-C (coupled Burgers test, GCC and Intel compilers), but the paper itself (arXiv 1709.07229, dl.acm.org) is blocked here, so no number, CPU or flag was seen. Kept at B on the peer-review precedent; the repo has no benchmark code, so A is not reachable from it.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Per search-result summaries of the TOMS paper (not opened): CoDiPack's tapes perform similarly to Adept, with tape memory reduced by 15% (1-argument statements) to 5% (4-argument statements) relative to Adept's Jacobian-taping layout, and the index-handling tapes cut reverse interpretation time; the comparison against ADOL-C (primal taping) is in the paper but its factors were not seen. No speedup figure was verified.

tier_reason: README and repo publish no timing; benchmark/ holds Google Benchmark sources (EnzymeCladComparison.cpp, Hessians.cpp, VectorModeComparison.cpp, GPT2Training.cpp, LULESH/XSBench patches) but no committed results. Kept (not rejected) because Clad is widely referenced as ROOT/RooFit's AD engine.

corrections.caveats: Evidence-free record: the repo ships benchmark code (benchmark/EnzymeCladComparison.cpp, built only with CLAD_ENABLE_ENZYME_BACKEND, plus Hessians.cpp, VectorModeComparison.cpp, GPT2Training.cpp built with -O3 -ffast-math, LULESH_diff.patch, XSBench_diff.patch, benchmark_compare.py) but no committed results; the Clad-vs-Enzyme benchmark compares two backends of Clad itself. Issue #1764 and PR #1771 (benchmark::DoNotOptimize fix for 0 ns results) are cited from the search record and were not re-opened. The ACAT 2022 paper 'Automatic Differentiation of Binned Likelihoods With RooFit and Clad' (arXiv 2304.02650) and the ROOT blog 'Automatic differentiation in RooFit with Clad' report, per search-result snippets only (arXiv, root.cern and indico.cern.ch blocked), TFormula gradient speedups of about 10x to 29x and a HistFactory minimization speedup of about 5.5x versus ROOT 6.26's numerical (finite-difference) gradients; that baseline is numerical differentiation, not another AD tool or a listed baseline, and the gain comes from reverse mode needing one sweep instead of n function calls. Tier D kept although the repo has fewer than 1k stars because Clad is the AD engine integrated in ROOT/RooFit at CERN.

notes: Metadata confirmed: LGPL-3.0 (License.txt), 421 stars, 212 forks, last commit 2026-09-30. If the orchestrator counts finite-difference gradients as a baseline, the ACAT 2022 paper could support B once opened; nothing against Adept, CppAD, CoDiPack or Enzyme has numbers.
